All hospitalised HIV-exposed children less than 6 months of age should be treated em- pirically with co-trimoxazole, unless HIV infection sta- tus is negative and the child is not being breast-fed. Em- pirical treatment with co-trimoxazole plus amoxicillin and an aminoglycoside should also be given to older HIV-infected children with features of AIDS who are not on co-trimoxazole prophylaxis • when Staph. aureus, is suspected, cloxacillin is the drug of choice. In HIV-infected children, about 60% of com- munity-acquired Staph. aureus may be resistant to cloxacillin and vancomycin should be given Hospital-acquired pneumonia. Most reports on hospital- acquired or nosocomial pneumonia have been from the USA. The organisms most commonly responsible for hos- pital-acquired pneumonia are Gram-negative enteric ba- cilli, Staph. aureus, Str. pneumoniae, Enterobacteriaceae, and H. influenzae; others that may need to be considered, particularly in the presence of specific risk factors, are Le- gionella spp., Ps. aeruginosa, anaerobes and, in severe in- fection, Acinetobacter spp. Hospital-acquired pneumonia occurring 48 hours after mechanical ventilation is termed ventilator-associated pneumonia; cases usually result from aspiration of pathogenic material that commonly colonises the oropharynx. The organisms often responsible for early onset ventilator-associated pneumonia are Staph. aureus, Str. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae while late-onset venti- lator-associated pneumonia is often caused by resistant nosocomial pathogens such as Ps. aeruginosa, meticillin resistant Staph. aureus, Klebsiella spp., and Acinetobacter baumannii.19 Broad spectrum antibacterial therapy is essential for hospi- tal-acquired pneumonia and most initial therapy is empiri- cal. As in the treatment of community-acquired pneumo- nia selection of antibacterials must be localised. For initial empirical treatment of early-onset hospital-acquired pneu- monia or ventilator-associated pneumonia in patients with no known risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens, and any disease severity, ATS recommends20 the follow- ing drugs: ceftriaxone; levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, or cip- rofloxacin; ampicillin/sulbactam; or ertapenem.
